On the darkest nights,  
When the moon sleeps,  
Or hides behind clouds,  
Look to the ridges,  
Do you see?  

The lights of their torches,  
One by one they come,  
Over the bare stone,  
Beneath the branches,  
Do you see?  

They are not gods,  
Oh no, no no no,  
They are the spirits of our ancestors,  
Warriors whose time has passed,  
Warriors who have forgotten,  
That the battles ever ended,  
Do you see?  

First the lights,  
Torches burning bright,  
Slowly move along the ridge,  
A distant drum fills the silence, 
The rhythm of their marching, 
Do you hear them?  

They are coming.

They walk the ancient paths,  
Toward battles long forgotten,  
Toward oaths kept sacred,  
Toward the living,  
Be warned!  

To look on them is death,  
To stand in their way is death,  
They seek the clear path,  
And where they find it…

*The bard paused, closing his fingers into a fist.*  

Taken!  

The elders knew,  
The door was the way,  
To ward off the spirits,  
Do you see?  

Look around!  
No home was safe,  
No fortress secure,  
If the way was clear,  
The Ancestor Spirits would come.

Friends!  
To this day no builder aligns doors,  
No path remains clear,  
From front to back,  
Do you see?

The wild ancestor of domestic cattle. Still present in the Heartlands, and still dangerous.
Forest edge, river valleys, open plains
Up to 11 ft long, 5 ft 10 in tall at the shoulder, 1,500 - 2,200 pounds
Passive at distance - dangerous when cornered or provoked

Wild aurochs and domestic cattle are the same animal at different points of the domestication process. Domestic breeding lines have been established long enough to produce reliably manageable stock, but the wild population persists in the Heartlands and should not be approached as though it shares the temperament of a barn animal.

## Physical Description

The aurochs is a massively built bovine, significantly larger than other cattle breeds. The body is deep-chested and heavily muscled, carried on legs built for rough terrain as much as open plain. The coat is dark brown to near-black in bulls, lighter in cows, with a pale stripe running the length of the spine. The horns sweep forward and upward from the skull in a wide arc, reaching up to three feet in length in mature bulls. The head is carried lower than domestic cattle, with a broad forehead and a directness to the gaze that experienced hunters describe as categorically different from domesticated stock.

## Wild Behavior

Aurochs are grazers and browsers occupying forest edge, river valley, and open plain across the Heartlands basin. They are not migratory in the way of cerostim but move seasonally across established ranges following forage and water. Herds are typically small - a dominant bull, several cows, and calves - with younger bulls moving in loose bachelor groups at the margins.

They are passive toward humans and most predators at distance. A cornered aurochs is a different problem. Bulls will charge without significant warning when threatened, and a direct hit from a mature bull has killed horses. Stone drakes take aurochs, but selectively - calves and isolated cows are preferred targets. A healthy bull is a serious undertaking even for a drake.

## Domesticated Behavior & Uses

Domestic cattle in the Heartlands are descended from aurochs stock and retain more of the wild type's size and temperament than breeds from more settled regions. They are used for meat, milk, hide, and draft labor as oxen. Calves taken young and raised in human company are manageable. Adult wild aurochs cannot be domesticated. Wild bulls occasionally challenge or infiltrate domestic herds, which presents both a management problem and a danger to handlers.

*Note unattributed - the author left no distinquishing markings but it appears to be addressed to the Imperial authorities rather than the Merchant Houses.*

I have now spent eleven days doing what I was asked to do, which was determine whether the maps left behind by our former Khuldinai contractors could serve as a foundation for a proper Imperial survey of the northern territories. I regret to inform the Ministry that they cannot, and I would like it noted for the record that I said as much before I ever opened the first crate, to anyone who would listen, which was no one.

The Khuldinai, in their infinite contractual precision, delivered exactly what their agreement specified: engineering services rendered, foundations laid, tunnels bored, the caldera walls assessed and reinforced where necessary. What their agreement did not specify, and what they therefore did not leave behind, was a single coherent map of anything. When I raised this with the Ministry's own solicitor, he informed me that the phrase "supporting documentation" does not appear in the original contract language, and that Khuldinai counsel anticipated this exact dispute and worded the agreement accordingly. They took their maps home. They left us the buildings and nothing that explains how the buildings relate to the land around them. I am told this was a very favorable contract for the Empire at the time it was signed. I would be curious to know for whom.

What remains in the archive is garbage, and I no longer say that as an assessment. I say it as a description.

I have catalogued thirty-one documents purporting to represent some portion of the northern territories. Four are drawn to a stated scale. The rest are drawn to whatever scale suited the artist's evident mood that day. Seven depict the same stretch of river with the same tributary entering from three different directions. Two disagree on whether a named lake exists at all. One depicts a mountain range as a single unbroken wall with a note in the margin reading "approximately here, more or less, ask a local." The document is forty years old. I could not locate the local. I am not certain the local ever existed, and at this point I am not certain the cartographer did either.

It gets worse. Having failed to reconcile these documents against one another, I brought a selection to the Temple, in the hope that some cleric with a stronger stomach for geography than mine might identify which were merely inaccurate and which were something else. Two were confirmed outright forgeries - invented wholesale by someone who had clearly never left the city, working from rumor and the desire to be paid for a commission they had no ability to complete. I do not fault them for their ambition. I fault the Ministry archive for filing their fabrication alongside genuine survey work for forty years without anyone checking.

The remainder, the Temple could not condemn as forgeries, and could not vouch for as accurate either. When I pressed the officiating cleric on how a document could be neither, she offered the opinion that the maps may well have been true when they were drawn, and that the land itself has since been redrawn by the gods for reasons known only to them. I do not know what I am meant to do with that assessment. I did not ask a second question, because I did not want a second answer.

I also consulted the Legion's mages, on the theory that whatever arts they employ for their scrying and their signal-work might be turned toward resolving a river's true course. I was informed, politely, that this is not what their arts are for, and less politely, that I was the third cartographer this decade to ask.

I have begun to suspect that most of these documents were never produced by anyone who set foot in the territory they claim to represent. The contradictions are too consistent in their wrongness, the way a rumor stays consistent as it travels - a river becomes a lake becomes a story becomes a line on a page, and no one along that chain ever checked it against the ground. It is almost as if someone drew these based on a tale they heard passed through several ears, rather than walking the land themselves, and I am forced to conclude that in at least two cases, that is precisely what happened, minus even the tale.

I recommend the following, in order of what I expect the Ministry will actually fund:

First, that a proper survey expedition be commissioned, because these documents cannot be reconciled - they were never describing the same reality to begin with, whatever the Temple wishes to believe about the gods' cartographic habits.

Second, failing that, that I be permitted to produce a single composite document clearly marked as speculative, so that no future officer mistakes our best guess for a verified record, the way I am now fairly certain several of my predecessors did, to the Empire's lasting inconvenience.

Third, that someone revisit our contract language with the Khuldinai, so that "supporting documentation" is no longer a phrase their counsel can turn against ours a second time.

I remain the Ministry's servant in this matter, for now.

The great deer of the Heartlands. Once migrated in herds from the northern mountains to the coast and back again.
Open plains, forest edge, mountain foothills
8 - 10 ft long, 6 - 7 ft tall at the shoulder, 1,100 - 1,500 pounds
Passive unless provoked - dangerous during rut

*Believed extinct in the Heartlands region. Unverified sighting reports persist from the northern ranges and eastern passes.*

Once the dominant megafauna of the Heartlands basin, the cerostim shaped the region's ecology and drew its first human settlers to the plain. Their absence defines the landscape as much as their presence once did.

## Physical Description

The cerostim is a large deer, heavier and taller than its forest-dwelling cousins, built for open ground and forest edge rather than dense cover. The body is heavily muscled beneath a coarse, dark brown coat that lightens along the flanks in winter. The legs are long and capable - a cerostim moving at pace crosses ground with a silence that observers consistently note as wrong for something of its size.

The antlers are the defining feature and occur only in mature bulls. They are palmate rather than branching, broad flat spans of bone with tines projecting from the outer edge, extending up to twelve feet tip to tip. The weight of a full rack approaches eighty to ninety pounds. Bulls carry their antlers with a characteristic high-set posture that keeps the span level and readable from a distance. Cows are antlerless and roughly three quarters the size of bulls.

## Wild Behavior

Cerostim are migratory herd animals, historically moving between northern mountain foothills and the southern coast in seasonal cycles. Herds traveled in the hundreds, following established routes across the Heartlands plain that remained consistent across generations. Individual animals are browsers and grazers both, adapting diet to available forage across the migration range.

They are passive toward most animals and humans outside of rut season. A bull in rut is a different animal entirely - territorial, aggressive, and capable of doing serious damage with both antlers and hooves. Hunters are advised to treat a rutting bull as an active threat regardless of provocation.

Stone drakes historically preyed heavily on cerostim during migration, timing their own seasonal activity to the herd movements. The collapse of cerostim populations in the Heartlands correspondingly stressed drake food supplies and altered drake ranging behavior.

## Domesticated Behavior & Uses

Cannot be domesticated. Historically the primary large game animal of the Heartlands, providing meat, hide, bone, and antler material. Antler spans were kept as trophies and status markers among hunting cultures.

Some call it magic, Visareen call it 'mana'. It is the energy that connects all things in the world.

*Musings on the nature of the worlds energies, compiled from notes in the Imperial Archives, including banned works.*

## The Flow Itself

The energy has no single name. The Empire calls it flow. The Visareen call it mana. Those without a framework call it magic. The Wildkin have no word for it at all - naming it would imply separation from it, and they recognize no such separation.

It moves through everything. Stone and bird and sky and soil, the living and the dead, the practitioner and the world being practiced upon. It streams and surfaces, dives underground and returns. It does not favor any single vessel or framework. It does not distinguish between the wizard drawing it through a mirror-bowl, the Temple healer asking to receive it, and the wind moving across an open plain.

The disagreement between institutions is not about the energy itself. It is about what relationship a person is permitted to have with it - extractive, devotional, integrative - and what that relationship says about the institution claiming it. The energy remains indifferent to all of them.

Those who have seen it clearly tend to stop arguing about frameworks.

## Legion Perspective

The Legion approaches flow, which it sometimes refers to generically as the world’s energy system, as a tool to be understood, assigned, and controlled. Every practitioner is evaluated before training and assigned to the discipline most aligned with their essence: scrying, conjuration, illusion, destruction, among others. 

The underlying mechanic is consistent across all disciplines: energy is drawn in from the world around the practitioner, stored briefly in the body, then focused and released toward a purpose.

The toll is real and cumulative. Scrying clouds the eyes and eventually milks them over. Combat mages burn fast and die young. Minds trained in silent speech develop waking echoes they can never fully quiet. Those who attempt to step between spaces sometimes emerge wrong in ways that are hard to name. When possible, the Legion mitigates this through object channeling - instruments that absorb the cost of channeling so the practitioner's body doesn't have to bear the full weight.

The Legion doesn't deny the danger. It manages it, allocates it, and sends the bill to whoever is least valuable. Any discipline is theoretically available to any practitioner willing to pay the cost. But the Legion discourages wandering outside assigned disciplines - not out of ignorance, but pragmatism. The cost of learning what you weren't built for tends to be paid in years.

## Temple Perspective

The Temple practitioners do not draw energy - they receives it. Where the Legion sees a resource to be extracted, the Temple's practitioners see themselves as vessels. Mana flows into them not because they reached for it, but because they asked, and were answered.

The discipline is devotional rather than technical. A Temple healer does not study the mechanics of restoration; they study the nature of the gods who favor it. The results are real - wounds close, fevers break, the dying sometimes don't - but the Temple attributes the mechanism entirely to divine will. That the gods might be channeling the same energy the Legion deploys through mirror-bowls and combat mages is not a question the Temple entertains seriously. The energy is a gift. Asking where it comes from is ingratitude.

## Wildkin Perspective

Where the Empire categorizes and contains, the Wildkin relationship to the world's energy is integrative rather than extractive. It flows through them as it flows through the land – the Visareen singing to stars even as their forests burn, the Somari moving through desert terrain with an intimacy no Imperial map can replicate. The Wildkin don't draw energy in and release it; they exist within it. 

## Unresolved Phenomena

Not everything mana does fits neatly into any framework. There are examples of mana interacting with the world without a practitioner directing it. Uncontrolled, ambient, sometimes dangerous.

The Legion files these under unsolved problems. The Temple attributes them to gods and restless spirits. The Wildkin, who live closest to the flow, tend to treat them as simply another natural phenomenon rather than miracle. None of the these formal frameworks fully accounts for them, and none of the institutions is comfortable admitting that.

## The Fall of Man

They say that in the age before ruin, mankind reached beyond the sky, daring to set foot on the moon with dreams of traveling to the stars beyond.  When they first reached pale lantern that drifts above the world, it gave them the confidence that they would not suffer the same fate as Icarus, they could defy the gods and leave this prison of ocean and dirt. For a time, it was believed the heavens themselves would be conquered, that the void would be their kingdom. But pride soured into discord, and soon the fires of envy burned hotter than the stars.
The mighty realms of men built strongholds upon the great lantern floating in the darkness. Each claimed it as their own, seeking to keep its resources for their people, or perhaps more accurately for their kings, and none would yield. Whispers tell of a gathering of men where oaths were broken, trust betrayed, and tempers flared. Not long after, war erupted – sudden, merciless, and without restraint. The fighting initially raged upon the lantern’s dust before infecting the skies above, and at last, upon the earth itself. Among the ruins of those battlegrounds, wanderers still say you can find stones melted into glass, too smooth to have come from any hand but fire from the sky.

## The Imperial Basin

The land immediately surrounding the great city is best understood not as a single terrain but as a series of concentric conditions, each one shaped by its proximity to the Dragon's Spine mountains at the city's back.

Timbur Deep sits where the volcanic range meets the plain, pressed against the mountain like a thing that grew there rather than was built. From the lower districts, the range reads as broad and grey, less impressive than its reputation suggests - a wall of dark stone and persistent cloud, unremarkable until the light changes or the season turns and the upper reaches hold snow while the valley floor is still warm. From the upper districts, closer to the mountain's foot, the impression corrects itself. The peaks are not small. The city simply makes them seem so from below.

The farmland that feeds the city spreads south and west from the mountain's shadow, following the two river systems that bracket the range on either side. The eastern river is the larger and more traveled of the two, running south from the high country before bending toward the sea. It is a quiet river in its lower reaches - broad, slow, the color of pewter on overcast days - and the land along its banks is dark and generous, the kind of soil that produces without argument. The western river is narrower and less celebrated, but no less important; it drains a separate basin entirely, and the redundancy is not accidental. The region between the two rivers, sheltered from the worst of the northern winds by the mountain's bulk, is among the most reliably productive land in the known world.

Supply moves along both rivers by barge. The eastern route is the longer and slower of the two, carrying the majority of what arrives from the coast. The western river supports a ferry system that reaches distant farms both north and west of the city. Neither route is swift, but both are dependable, and dependability is worth more than speed when you are feeding four hundred thousand people.

The dark mountain range itself - the volcanic spine that gives the city its character - is not a place for settlements. It is too steep, too irregular, too full of the kind of terrain that swallows expeditions and returns nothing. The stone is young by geological measure, sharp where it should be rounded, hollow where it should be solid. Travelers who have entered it in any depth describe a landscape that does not behave consistently - drainage that runs the wrong direction, passes that close without warning, drops that appear without preamble. Bandits work it. Larger things work it too. The city's garrison does not pursue either very far in.

The cold continental air begins losing ground to the warming sea air in early spring, and the transition is rarely polite. The ridgelines catch whatever breeze exists; the valley floors do not. Storm season runs through midsummer - fast-moving systems that build over the sea, push north, and release hard over the basin before dissipating against the northern and eastern ranges. The storms arrive with little warning and pass quickly, leaving the air briefly clean before the humidity reasserts itself.

*Autumn*

The balance tips back toward the continental air as the sea cools. Mornings turn cold fast while afternoons stay warm long enough to be deceptive. Fog is the defining feature of autumn in the Heartlands - cold air sliding down from the ridges at night hits the warmer valley floor air and stays there until midday. Harvest happens in this light: flat, grey-white, diffuse. The ridgeline farms finish before the valley farms, which finish before the river-bottom farms.

The continental air reasserts fully and the Heartlands argues with it rather than surrendering to it. Snow arrives in events - a hard fall that blankets the basin, sits for a week or two, then a warm pulse from the south clears it. Then another fall. The city never fully locks into winter the way the high range does; it cycles in and out of it. The dramatic quality of the snow is partly elevation - the caldera rim over Timbur Deep holds white for months while the valley floor below is already wet and grey again. When both air masses are present simultaneously and in roughly equal strength, the Heartlands gets its worst weather: sustained heavy snowfall, then immediate thaw, then freeze again as the continental air returns. The infrastructure knows this pattern. The roads are built for it. New arrivals are not.

As told by the wind-singers of the Somari people.

No one remembers the name he carried when they caught him, only that he was not from their land. Skin soft from city shade. Eyes too tired to fear the wind.

He was bound like any other and tossed into the cage, left to wait for a better death, one the elders could bless.

But the spirits heard him first.

When the moon was a sliver too thin to cast a shadow, the beast came. Not great and mighty, no.

A small thing.

It wore stripes and a mask. Eyes like wet coals and hands too clever to belong to a beast.

Each night the conjurer summoned the trickster. Each night they hunted it. Each night it hissed like wind through bone and vanished into smoke.

On the third night, the child watched as he summoned the beast for a final time.

The conjurer had been stripped bare, but still he summoned the beast. Through pain and fire, it burst from his shoulders. And by morning, he was gone.

The elders claim it was not a beast, but a companion. A spirit of the in-between. A creature of cunning and teeth and quiet escapes. It chose him, not the other way around.
Since then, the warriors leave bits of raw sinew and cracked bone outside their tents. An offering to the spirit to make amends.

## On the Reckoning of Days and Seasons
*From the Great House Trade Treaty, distributed to factors and agents across the Empire. Year 753 of the Common Reckoning.*

---

A merchant who cannot name the season has no business calling himself a Great House. We record this not to instruct the learned, but because experience has shown that agents arriving from the western territories - and on occasion from among our Visari partners, who track time by altogether different customs - may benefit from a plain account of the calendar as it is observed within the Empire.

The Common Reckoning holds twelve moons to a year. This is the number the Empire counts, the number the taxmen write into their ledgers, and the number by which the Great Houses schedule contracts. The year 753 CR begins, as all years do, with the cold.

Each season turns on its midpoint. The deep of winter, the height of summer, the precise balance of spring and autumn - these are not the beginnings of their seasons but the pivots. A farmer in the Heartlands does not need a scholar to tell him when winter starts; he knows it when the ground freezes and his breath fogs. The equinoxes and solstices mark the turning of the wheel, not its first spoke.

This is worth understanding for practical reasons. A contract specifying delivery *before the solstice* means before the peak of summer, not before summer begins. Agents who confuse pivot for threshold have cost this house money. We note it plainly.

A discussion on the systems that govern the Empire.

*As understood by Rast, Wizard of the Tower and conjurer of woodland spirits.*

The Empire, as we know it, is unlike the empires of old. The Emperor is a figure whose voice carries weight, but he is not the ultimate authority in the land. The engine that powers the imperial apparatus is derived from four largely independent components. I shall describe them here, based on my experience of each.

## The Four Pillars

If we think of the Empire as the surface of a table, each of the individual components underneath provide support like legs. If we take any single one out, it creates instability that threatens the whole.

The Emperor is the figurehead. The Councilors, and there are twelve of them, are appointed advisors. Combined, they are responsible for setting administrative policies within the Empire’s sphere of influence, and for negotiations with external forces like the Visari and Khuldinai. The Emperor rules by decree - his authority backed by the Legion and threat of violence.

The Legion is the Empire’s enforcement arm - it is deployed with diplomacy fails. Legion deployments are directed by the Emperor, supplied by the Merchant Houses, and sanctioned by the Temple. The Legion is the pillar I am most familiar with, and I shall describe it in further detail in a moment.

The Temple is the divine sanctioning organization within the Empire, and of the four pillars it is the one I understand least and trust the least. It is not a single religion - it is an organization that services multiple faiths under one institutional roof, which tells you more about its function than its theology. Where the Legion controls through violence and the Merchant Houses through resources, the Temple controls through something harder to quantify: the internalized belief that certain behaviors are sanctioned by powers higher than any Emperor. For many, that is the highest authority they will ever answer to. The Temple also provides moral sanction for Legion deployments - a Legion excursion blessed by the Temple is a righteous act, while one conducted without that blessing is just violence, which the Empire prefers to avoid framing it as. I will note that the Temple's influence is uneven - within the Bastion it may outrank a Councilor in a specific circumstance, while in the Slums it thins considerably. The old gods have not finished losing yet.

The Merchant Houses are the economic engine that underpins everything else. They move grain and supplies, and may be more diplomatically important than the Empire’s direct servants. Their influence reaches far beyond the Empire’s official borders and their primary concern is centered around profit.

Together, these Four Pillars dictate every policy, trade, and everyday life of the Empire’s subjects.

## Interdependency

Despite being independent organizations, each of the Pillars is dependent on the others. The Legion depends on the Empire for funding, which then gets directed to Merchant Houses for supplies. The Merchant Houses rely on the Legion to ensure trade routes stay clear of threat, human or otherwise. The Temple provides moral guidance and justifies the Emperor’s decrees and sanctions Legion excursions. The Emperor, in turn, is able to use the Temple to focus any discontent away from the Emperor and the Councilors, redirecting toward unseen divine forces. While it may seem then, that the Emperor or Temple may serve as a high authority, the Legion has its own mandate that allows, nay, requires it to depose leadership that no longer serves the Empire’s interests.

Everything any of these organizations do must effectively maintain the whole, otherwise instability threatens everyone.

But, you ask, whose authority is highest?

The truth is - it depends.

Within the Bastion and higher echelons of Timbur Deep, a Temple agent may carry more authority in a specific circumstance than a Councilor. In the Slums, the Legion may carry the most authority through the capacity for violence. Each organization has exactly as much authority in any given situation as anyone else allows. Ultimately, the Pillars work together for the good of the Empire.

At least, the good of the people in power.

## Regional Lordship and Domains

As I mentioned earlier, the Empire is not a monolithic organization like the empires of worlds past. Rather, it maintains a loose grip over a region dominated by largely independent administrative zones which are collectively referred to as “Domains”. This term came to be used as they are too small to be referred to as independent kingdoms, but the Empire cares not to impose its culture and political structure downward.

What this has created is a network of Domains whose political systems may differ greatly depending on what the people of that region want for themselves. In most, a Lord is declared and succession is determined through direct lineage. In others, leadership may fall to the eldest member of the tribal group. Another still may attempt to organize their Domain into a council or even, gods, a democracy of sorts.

In any case, the Empire has demands of the Lords of each Domain: taxes must be paid, stability must be maintained, Legion movement must be unrestricted. Beyond that, the Empire doesn’t care about how the Lords choose to live and organize themselves. Stability is paramount, and anything that threatens the stability of the Empire is dealt with swiftly and violently.

The cleverness of this system is twofold. First, it allows the Empire to maintain control over a large territory without incurring the expense of maintaining occupying forces across the region or imposing its own cultural values on a civilian population that values autonomy. Second, by sanctioning each Domain to develop its own system of governance, it offers the residents a feeling of independence while providing a layer of protection against external threats.

This system, the Empire has found, has proven less problematic than prior Empires who faced routine invasion, rebellion, and wars of independence.

## Standing Armies and Legion Mandates

Worth noting is that while each Domain is semi-autonomous, the Empire has established a policy of restricting each Lord from establishing any significant standing military force. Each is allowed a certain garrison to serve as immediate protection for the people, but any attempt by a Lord to establish their own army quickly results in the Merchant Houses draining resources from the Domain, which usually motivates the Lord back into compliance. Thus, while each Domain may have their own local militia and guards, none ever grow to a size that threatens the authority of the Empire.

The Legion is the exception - it is the officially sanctioned army of the Empire that serves not as an occupation force, but as a force designed for rapid deployment to problematic areas. This may be to settle a dispute between rival Lords that could not be resolved diplomatically or economically, or to exterminate any non-human threats that may disrupt local stability. It is this promise of rapid, extreme violence that ensures compliance with Imperial mandates, and for most people, that is enough.

To maintain this relationship, Legion in service of local Lords, each Domain is assigned a Prefect. The Prefect is a Legion officer that serves as a liaison between the Lord and the Legion directly, without requiring the Emperor’s involvement. The Prefect works with local agents from the Merchant Houses to keep track of resources in the region that are critical to the functioning of the Empire, manages a spy network to detect early indicators of instability, and maintains oversight of the Lords management of their Domain. Any Lord whose policies and behaviors begin to disturb the region may receive gentle correction and guidance through the Prefect, Temple, or Merchant Houses.

## *Deposition*

There are times, however, when a Lord may simply choose to be difficult and assert themselves in a manner no longer in the best interests of the Empire. In those rare cases, the Legion has the explicit mandate to perform a *Deposition* of the existing Lord. Legion soldiers are deployed, the Lord is removed through the most extreme means available, and a new Lordship is established. The preference toward extreme violence, in which case the entire ruling family may be brutally executed in a most public way, is intended to serve as judgement on the failed Lord and a warning to other Lords of the fate that awaits them should they also be found wanting in service of the Empire.

Council-based Lordships deserve special attention here. It could be assumed that without a single point of accountability the strategy would not be effective. That is wrong. The entire council is executed and replaced. In a democracy, everyone in a position of accountability is deposed. The brutality of it creates a self-policing model where even in systems of distributed leadership, each member has a vested interest in holding each other accountable.

Deposition is performed without requiring explicit sanctioning from the other Pillars. In truth, by the time a Deposition is necessary it is highly likely that the other Pillars would agree with the act as their own efforts to correct the Domain have failed. What remains behind depends on the political structure that was deposed. A lineage-based Lordship may simply have the problematic member removed and leadership passes to the next in line, while a council-based Lordship may require the people to come together to resolve the issue.

Crucially, it is important to understand that even a kind and well-meaning Lord may suffer Deposition. The Empire cares about stability, and if the Lord's influence isn't enough to keep usurpers and dissidents at bay, then he will be deemed ineffective in serving the Empire. A Lord, therefore, can never afford to be neither too cruel nor too kind if they are to govern effectively.

## *Abeyance*

Whatever the reason for Deposition, the Legion, in collaboration with the Merchant Houses and Temple, will assume control of strategic resources within the Domain until a new Lordship is established. This is generally accomplished within a week as someone will often have been selected to replace the Lord beforehand, but in some cases that may not be possible.

If the new Lordship is not established within the appointed time period, the Legion will employ a strategy termed *Abeyance*. To put it simply - the Legion will withdraw its forces from the region aside from the protection of the assets deemed to be most strategically important to the Empire. This is the least desirable state for the Domain to fall into as the power vacuum generates instability that wreaks havoc on the local people.

While this may seem cruel, it is a strategic calculation of the Empire that assures the instability will be resolved quickly by the local people, without requiring the Empire’s resources. Merchant Houses, in particular, will be eager to establish a new Lordship to restore stability and economic activity. They already know which resources matter and why, and are therefore uniquely positioned to facilitate a new Lordship quickly. The people as well have a particular interest in restoring order. Without a Lordship respected by the Empire, they receive no resources, no security, and are cut off from external supply lines. The Empire uses patience as a weapon, letting attrition and suffering do the work of motivating people toward a stable Lordship rather than going through the expense of forcing one upon them.

In short - people die, often in great numbers. And the Empire believes it can outlast the chaos while the people reorganize.

The Legion mandate of Deposition isn’t just reserved for the Domain Lords, it applies to the Empire as well. Should the Emperor himself or the Councilors be found unfit to serve the interest of the Empire, they too risk Deposition.

Through this mechanism the Empire maintains control over the various semi-autonomous Domains. The Merchant Houses influence the Legion, and the Legion ensures even the Emperor does what’s best for the survival of the Empire.

## Parting Thoughts

The system creates a delicate power balance that doesn’t favor any single entity. Instead, interdependence ensures that each entity has sufficient motivation to engage in behaviors that best serve the Empire. The Empire setting policy, Merchant Houses controlling resources, Temple influencing the population, and Legion's threat of violence create a self-monitoring system that does not allow any single entity to stray too far without extreme risk. For most in positions of power, it's better to stay comfortable than risk everything in a power grab.

A colleague of mine said it best when I asked him what he thought was the most important thing to remember:

*“Whatever keeps the Empire on top.”*

In truth, by the time a Deposition is necessary it is highly likely that the other Pillars would agree with the act as their own efforts to correct the Domain have failed. What remains behind depends on the political structure that was deposed. A lineage-based Lordship may simply have the problematic member removed and leadership passes to the next in line, while a council-based Lordship may require the people to come together to resolve the issue.

Crucially, it is important to understand that even a kind and well-meaning Lord may suffer Deposition. The Empire cares about stability, and if the Lord’s influence isn’t enough to keep usurpers and dissidents at bay, then he will be deemed ineffective in serving the Empire. A Lord, therefore, can never afford to be neither too cruel nor too kind if they are to govern effectively.

Whatever the reason for Deposition, the Legion, in collaboration with the Merchant Houses and Temple, will assume control of strategic resources within the Domain until a new Lordship is established. This is generally accomplished within a week as someone will often have been selected to replace the Lord beforehand, but in some cases that may not be possible.

If the new Lordship is not established within the appointed time period, the Legion will employ a strategy termed Abeyance. To put it simply - the Legion will withdraw its forces from the region aside from the protection of the assets deemed to be most strategically important to the Empire. This is the least desirable state for the Domain to fall into as the power vacuum generates instability that wreaks havoc on the local people.

While this may seem cruel, it is a strategic calculation of the Empire that assures the instability will be resolved quickly by the local people, without requiring the Empire’s resources. Merchant Houses, in particular, will be eager to establish a new Lordship to restore stability and economic activity. They already know which resources matter and why, and are therefore uniquely positioned to facilitate a new Lordship quickly. The people as well have a particular interest in restoring order. Without a Lordship respected by the Empire, they receive no resources, no security, and are cut off from external supply lines. The Empire uses patience as a weapon, letting attrition and suffering do the work of motivating people toward a stable Lordship rather than going through the expense of forcing one upon them.

In short - people die, often in great numbers. And the Empire believes it can outlast the chaos while the people reorganize.

The Legion mandate of Deposition isn’t just reserved for the Domain Lords, it applies to the Empire as well. Should the Emperor himself or the Councilors be found unfit to serve the interest of the Empire, they too risk Deposition.

The system creates a delicate power balance that doesn’t favor any single entity. Instead, interdependence ensures that each entity has sufficient motivation to engage in behaviors that best serve the Empire. The Empire setting policy, Merchant Houses controlling resources, Temple influencing the population, and Legion’s threat of violence create a self-monitoring system that does not allow any single entity to stray too far without extreme risk. For most in positions of power, it’s better to stay comfortable than risk everything in a power grab.

## 17th Day of Hearthkeep, Year 701 CR

It feels like years ago when Lord Niven first proposed independence, and at the time it was inconceivable. Since then we’ve watched. We’ve counted. We’ve followed every Imperial request without deviation. I believe we’ve covered every possible outcome.  

The Empire cares little for our Domain. It does not ask for tribute like many other Domains, and it does not seem intent on maintaining a permanent Legion garrison here. In fact, outside of occasional Imperial representatives that come to research the surrounding mountains, we see very little of the Empire’s people.  

We just need to decide what to do with Prefect Baelyn. Tegan thinks we should let the Prefect know ahead of time and convince him to join us. I think Tegan is a bit naïve and his kindness is going to get him into trouble.

## 29th Day of Hearthkeep, Year 701 CR

This is it!  

Lord Niven has decided and the council agreed – we shall begin the next year as a fully independent nation no longer subservient to the Empire. In two days we will inform Prefect Baelyn and order the Legion out.  

All hail the Kingdom of Darnay! 

## 1st Day of Frostbreak, Year 702 CR

The independent Kingdom of Darnay has been founded!  

We worried much for so little. The Prefect barely contested our declaration, and simply asked if we were sure.  

Yes Prefect, we are sure. We are sure and we are free!  

## 8th Day of Frostbreak, Year 702 CR

The transition of power went as smoothly as any of us could have predicted. We did not need to raise arms, and there was no bloody conflict as the rumors suggested. King Niven secured more than 400 warriors to protect the village, but the Prefect simply… left. As did the other Legion soldiers. We expected more fight from the Empire. Perhaps it is weaker than we thought.

Our only challenge came from House Kittis. The Master of Coin warned about some vague calamity or such nonsense. I think he is just nervous and has never tasted true freedom.  

There is a crispness to the air that feels invigorating, and long overdue.  

## 16th of Meltwater, Year 702 CR

It has been several weeks now since our independence, and as I look around I must admit that not much has changed. The people still gather for warm drinks. They laugh and sing as they always have. The Nirashi still visit to entertain or provide trade services.  

Even House Kittis has come to terms with our independence, and they have voiced no further complaint.  

Perhaps it is due to the cold lingering on the ground, or that we are still adjusting to the new order. In any case, it feels like nothing is different, and everything is different. It’s an odd sensation and I could not point to the cause, or the outcome.  

I’m rambling. Perhaps I am too happy with drink.  

## 8th of Furrowdeep, Year 702 CR

Plowing and field preparation have resumed. King Niven has ordered a celebration for two weeks from now, and tasked me to secure enough ale to ensure the mugs never run dry. I must speak with House Kittis. The roads should be clear enough soon to bring in what we need.  

Oddly, when we announced the celebration the villagers didn’t respond with the enthusiasm we expected. Some even seemed skeptical of a celebration. But King Niven insisted that such a monumental event should be celebrated, and I agree.  

Tegan, ever the kind heart, volunteered to craft a crown wrought iron and precious stones for the new King.

## 23rd of Furrowdeep, Year 702 CR

It is with heavy heart that I record this passage, and I do so only so that future generations will remember what happened and, perhaps, seek vengeance.  

The King has been slain.  

I still cannot believe it.  

We had the village secured with more than 300 soldiers. Armed. Ready.

King Niven personally had six of the best warriors at his side.

It didn’t matter. The Legion is Legion.

I will explain as best I can.

It happened during the Celebration of Independence. The great hall was full of village elders, farmers, Darnay’s most important people. The King’s own mage, Cinnaren, sat at a large table to the side, using his skills to watch for threats to the King, suppressing other energies in the room. He made sure the King was safe.  

Legion struck him first.  

An assassin’s arrow came from a high alcove, entering his throat from the side and sinking into his chest. A moment later, I only heard a sickening crunch to my side. When I looked, a wooden stake had burst forth from King Niven’s chest. He tried to cry out, a scream drowned in blood. Seconds later, each of the elite guards had been dispatched, throats slit with obsidian blades. Behind me, a Legion mage had passed through the wall to stand behind the slain King.  

I don’t mean he came through a door. He came through the fucking wall like a ghost!  

Without Cinnaren’s protection, the Legion mage had reshaped the King’s chair into a spike driven through his heart!

It happened too fast. Less than the blink of an eye. None of us moved. The Legion had arrived in the way the rumors said it would. Not with a column of soldiers flying Imperial banners.  

Like lightning.  
Like vengeance.   
Like a god offended.  

By morning, Legion soldiers had established a presence in the village. We were too shocked by the suddenness, the brutality, to fight back. There was no violence beyond the initial strike. Legion soldiers offered no offenses, and our own soldiers simply accepted their presence. They didn’t patrol like an invading army, rather, they occupied specific locations with the claim of ensuring order.  

Prefect Baelyn requested an audience in the center of the village. None declined.  

He told us we had exactly seven days to select a new Lord, or to decide how we would rule ourselves in service of the Empire. The Kingdom of Darnay was no more. The Domain of Darnay reestablished.  

## 28th of First Seed, Year 702 CR

I am scared. I feel the Empire’s blade at my throat, and cannot do anything to push it off.  

No one can agree on how to move forward. Half of the village wants to fight for independence again, the other half wants to return to the old way.  I believe if we can hold out longer, we can regain independence when the Legion leaves the Domain.

House Kittis says we need to decide soon or things will get worse. I asked how that could be the case if the Legion’s policy was to hold territory for a short time, then leave. He shook his head at me and didn’t answer.

To his credit, Prefect Baelyn has kept his word. Legion soldiers have ensured there has been no crime since the King’s demise. Farms are still peaceful farms. Shops are still serviceable.  

I am living in a bizarre world where everything is the same, except we have eight fewer residents than a few days ago.  

In retrospect, the Nirashi have also gone missing. I am not sure exactly when they left, but they are not here now.

## 29th of First Seed, Year 702 CR

We did it!  

I was worried it was a lie, but the Prefect ordered Legion troops out of Darnay on this day. We are now free again and can rejoice!  

All hail the Kingdom of Darnay!

## 4th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

I am proud of our people. We have proven that we do not need an Empire to cast judgement, to watch over us. We are perfectly capable of governance on our own.  

With the Legion’s absence, our own warriors have volunteered to secure trade routes, and the people help each other freely. There have been some disagreements, but they are easily resolved through conversations.

## 6th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

The heat must be getting to people, they are starting to behave unreasonably. One villager tried to steal from the Kingdom’s food stores, and was caught by the blacksmith Tegan. Some want to remove his hand for the offense, some his feet. I have convinced them to allow the thief to work off the debt, but now some are looking at me differently.  

House Kittis brought in additional guards, for which I am grateful. Their assistance will be helpful in keeping the village peaceful.

## 9th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

House Kittis has betrayed us!  

We believed their guards were here to help. Instead, their guards were here to help House Kittis remove its networks from the village. Their warehouse and all their goods have disappeared virtually overnight. Along with them, other traders are now avoiding the Domain, and some things have become harder to obtain.  

No matter, we do not need any outside help.  

## 16th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

Supply shortages are starting to add pressure to the village. Some of the villagers are having difficulty finding clothes, and we’ve had to try to mine our own iron in the nearby mountains. It has proven difficult, but I am sure we will master the techniques soon.  

Grain stores are dwindling as well – we have not had any new shipments into the village since the King’s assassination. This is a problem that must be resolved sooner rather than later.  

## 25th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

Someone was murdered. I do not know her name, but the villagers are furious. She was a farmer’s wife, and the allegations claim she was murdered by a guard. The allegations further claim the guard murdered her because she refused his advances. I have been asked to provide a ruling. I wish it was not me.  

I do not want to be crowned King.  

I have seen what happens to Kings.  

## 28th of High Sun, Year 702 CR

The village is on the verge of anarchy. The people no longer help each other. Brutes with enough force take what they want and leave nothing for others. Several factions are forming, some well-trained. We have rumors of some being funded or directed by Houses of ill-repute, or worse.

I have asked those of noble intent to stand with me to protect the peace. I have heard of no less than twelve assaults against women since the assassination, and witnessed several attempted personally.  

Even Tegan, my friend, my council in dark times…  

I cannot bear to write it.  

## 2nd of Grainhead, Year 702 CR

The crops are failing. They are being raided faster than they can grow, even when they are not ready for harvest. We are incapable of defending our lands from raiders coming from other territories.  We are incapable of feeding ourselves. Incapable of producing iron. Incapable of making cloth. We have been cut off from nearly all trade. The only visitor to our village now is death.  

Still, I am proud of our people.  

## 5th of Grainhead, Year 702 CR

I have seen enough suffering.  

I have sent word to Prefect Baelyn.  

All hail the Domain of Darnay!

## The Nira People
I have learned much about the Nirashi since joining them some weeks ago in Moonglade. I have learned that, even among themselves, they are a mystery.  

The Nirashi do not know where they come from. Their oldest stories begin with motion – crossing a range, sheltering in a valley, moving on. They do not have a homeland, no record of what came before, no golden age. Most would experience this as a type of grief, a lack of belonging. To the Nira people, it is simply the shape of who they are.  

It follows, then, that the Nirashi accumulate things because they must. Portable wealth is the only kind available to a people who own no property, and it shows in how they travel. Layered textiles, decorated pack animals, and metalwork announce a Nirashi caravan at a distance. Jewelry and ornamentation become security, a currency that can be worn and traded. What a settled people build into walls, a Nirashi wears on their body, or embed into their covered cart-homes.  

They are a resourceful people, I have learned. They harvest wool and hide from wild stock in the mountains, deep in terrain most people don’t survive long enough to learn. The wool especially carries a quality unlike anything a settled weaver produces, and is renowned for its durability. They drive their caravans up to places where the trees meet the clouds, then continue on foot high above. They return with their spoils before nightfall, and everything is shared within the clan.  

But the Nirashi are adept at more than just the hunt. I have witnessed their connection to the world’s energies in wonder. To say that they are fortune tellers would be inaccurate, and is a myth held primarily by those who do not know them. Rather, they see shapes. The shape of things that were, and things that are. One of their elders told me that this is what allows them to clear the fog of the future, like a sculptor chipping away the stone to reveal a statue. It’s not that they know how to make dreams come true, despite what some might believe.  

They were the first to use objects to channel mana. Another claim they’ve laid before me, though this I would remain skeptical of. It is, however, a practice so ingrained into their culture that the tools have become highly associated with their people, and the art of divination. Reflective bowls, thick paper cards with elaborate drawings, smooth bones cast on the floor… It’s understandable that some mistake them for wildkin or shaman.  

Nirashi groups vary enormously in character. One may resemble a traveling merchant family, another a group of entertainers. Some focus on the hunt, and even offer services as mercenaries, if they don’t run off with your coin. What connects them is an uneasy comfort with impermanence, something most settled people recognize without being able to name directly.

## Nirashi Politics

A very interesting fact I have learned about them is they are both independent, and not independent clans at the same time. Each group organizes itself, often gifting authority to whoever has demonstrated the most useful combination of wisdom, competence, and survival. Elder women hold a disproportionate influence in most groups, though this varies. Within this independence, there is still a sense of belonging between one group and the next. I have witnessed this personally on several occasions when the caravans have run across each other. They trade while enjoying food and drink, and even sing songs they all seem to know, even if it was their first time crossing paths.

Their relationship to Imperial law requires an interpretation of philosophy. The Empire requires taxes, stability, and freedom of Legion movement, concerning itself with almost nothing else. Laws and policies beyond that are left to the Domain Lords and local custom. The Nirashi hold no land to impede the Legion, and pay no taxes. Therefore, they sit outside of that framework entirely. They do not break the Empire’s law because the Empire’s law does not reach them. What the Domain Lords think about this is the Domain Lord’s problem.  

How the Domains view the Nirashi varies by region and by who benefits from their presence. Where Merchant Houses dominate trade and local interests, they are viewed with suspicion. Even when they haven’t proven themselves to be disruptive or untrustworthy, the simple fact that they live outside the social contract presents problems. A Domain Lord cannot simply send their guards to deal with a Nirashi caravan the same way they could with a defiant farmer because the Nirashi caravan may not exist by the time the guards arrive. Once wealth becomes mobile, it becomes nearly impossible to tax reliably.  

In other regions, the Nirashi may be of great assistance to the local Domain Lord and earn their favor. Whether relying on their ability to bring in valuable supplies or use their divination skills to root out enemies, the Nirashi have made themselves invaluable in places where conventional services fail.

## Nirashi Traders

The Nirashi trade in things that travel well and require no fixed location. Crafted goods, medicinal preparations, divination services, information, and the movement of goods that settled traders cannot or will not handle. Their attunement to the world’s patterns makes them reliable readers of futures and routes - a Nirashi who says a pass will be dangerous next week has usually been right before.

Among their most distinctive trade goods are the products of mountain hunting. The Nirashi hunt the wild sheep of the upper ranges - sure-footed animals that descend into the valleys in winter and retreat above the treeline when the weather breaks. The hide and wool taken from these animals is unlike anything produced from domestic stock: coarser, denser, weatherproof in ways that farmed wool is not. The horn is worked into tools, vessels, and bow reinforcement. The meat, slow-cooked with high-elevation herbs gathered along the same routes, produces a meal with a flavor that settled cooks cannot replicate - not because the recipe is secret, but because the ingredients don’t exist below a certain altitude.

They are not wealthy by Imperial measure. They are also not dependent on Imperial systems to survive, which is a different kind of security - one that no amount of taxation or political pressure has yet managed to remove.

## The Sandborn Wedding

My Brother Darrel,  

Congratulations on your betrothal!  

We are most excited for the alliance of the Houses, as I believe it will bring great opportunity to access the rare dyes and sap of the great northern trees, and allow us to ship our glass much deeper into the Heartlands. I trust that you have already decided the colors for your wedding? Do let us know at your earliest convenience, as it can take some time to import the silks and get them dyed the right colors.  

My wife was glad to hear that Mina had already been living our ways for some time before your meeting. It was always difficult to get outsiders to understand the importance in jewelry, why detailed stitching matters. They often do not understand us when we say that one’s presentation should be representative of status, that a fancy palace or keep does not follow you to new places, and how other markers dissolve in the silt. The golden details in the dress she wore to meet us told us immediately that she understood.  

As to the other matters you wrote about, yes, the wells are still a problem. Every day we send our cousins under the water, they scoop the silt, and we toss it to the side. It takes hours to clear the bottom enough to ensure the cistern will refill itself for the next day. The Imperial Mathias claims the Khuldinai can make improvements so we do not have to dig, but their demands are outrageous!  

On the subject of Mathias, he continues to press on the issue of the varad. As you know, we thought the Empire was trying to deprive us of servants, insists that they are slaves, but as it turns out, they simply do not want us to call them that. They prefer we refer to them as “employees” or “servants”, as the word “slave” has become foul within the Empire. I have told him that we do not care what the Empire wants to call a vassal, we are not bound by their sensitivities.  

I find the whole affair amusing. The Empire is all too eager to conscript someone into service, bind them with debts, or ensure they earn just enough to eat and sometimes less. How is that not the same thing?  At least in our Houses we provide clean clothing, food, and shelter for our slaves. It is far better treatment than the Empire gives its own *free* people.  

Free. The hypocrisy. I have seen the Slums of the city, and if I were forced to choose, I would prefer to be a varad in the desert than a free person in the city.  

Enough of that. Your aunt Delpha said to remind you that you promised to write, and hadn’t. Or at least, she hasn’t received any messages. So please, brother, write to her. She has been terribly sad since you left and though she will not say it out loud, you were the favorite among us.  

Do give my regards to Mina, and don’t forget to send me the list of colors. Your wedding shall be a celebration to remember!

Regards,
Yazan

*Paraphrased excerpts from the work titled “People of the Western Steppe”, by Historian Valriss, Imperial Scholar.*

Considered by many to be savages, the Somari simply live outside the rules that bind societies like the Empire. They are a people defined by movement, rarely building permanent settlements and working with the land. They emphasize “the hunt”, and rely on herd animals that graze on the wild grassland rather than needing to be fed through farming. The Empire views the people as a problem to be managed, and not without merit. Raiding is a common practice among the Somari when trade agreements break down. Crucially, they are a collection of independent clans or tribes and not a unified nation. That works perfectly well for the people, and it keeps the Empire from having to contend with a strong adversary state full of people trained for combat from birth.

Mobility of the people is by design. The Plains of Somaria are home to more than just people, and makes for poor farmland. The people circulate legends of great beasts roaming parts of the plains or flying through the skies. Permanent settlements simply represent a food supply for such beasts, and the people have decided that is not a viable survival strategy. So they wander, moving their camps periodically with their herds, and do not become attached to any particular place.

Somari politics is a mystery to the author. They exist outside of Imperial territory, and do not document their philosophies. It is therefore nearly impossible to determine how the clans relate to each other, how they established any hierarchy, and how they manage trade between groups. What is known is that they appear to be matriarchal, or at least the elder women have a special place in their clans, doing as they see fit and others follow.

Trade with the Somari may be one of the more important considerations for those who live near them. It is important that they see your existence as valuable, otherwise an outsider is simply viewed as another type of beast, a threat to their existence. They are known to engage in raiding as another type of hunt. This practice creates significant instability for Merchant Houses along western supply routes. In fact, the author surmises that were it not for the great cliffs separating the Plains of Somaria from the Heartlands, they would pose a much greater threat to Imperial stability than they currently do.

The Somari provide meaningful resources to the Empire and the Merchant Houses. Horses trained by the clans are fearless mounts in combat, and some Somari warriors have found gainful employment among other groups. Their archers are among the finest in the lands, and they have a reputation for fearlessness that even seasoned warriors struggle to comprehend.

What the author hasn’t been able to describe is the Somari relationship to *ownership* - of the land, the people, the herds. Who speaks for them and how that is determined. The author concludes that more time must be spent in the region to understand the Somari, but declined to volunteer for that assignment.

Research Notes on the Subject of Death
Personal notes, compiled in service of Aldric's investigation into unconfirmed phenomena. For Temple use only.

I have been asked to compile what is known, and what is rumored, about the energetic remnants of the dead. Aldric was characteristically sparse in his instructions. 

*"Write down what you find. Leave nothing out. Especially the things that embarrass you."* 

I will do my best.

It is the Temple's position, and my own sincere belief, that the gods are present in all things. What follows does not contradict that. If anything, it confirms it - that even in death, even in suffering, something of the divine order persists. Whether that order is merciful is a question above my station.

## On Shades

The most common phenomenon reported to the Temple, and the most benign. A shade is not a presence - it is an impression. Witnesses describe seeing figures repeat the same action, walk the same path, speak without sound. The figures do not respond to intervention. They do not acknowledge the living. They simply... continue until they don't.

My understanding is that a shade is what remains when the energy of a moment is somehow fixed in place rather than released. A death, a great joy, a terrible violence - something caused the current to eddy rather than flow. What we observe is the echo of it, replaying without purpose or awareness.

The Temple's guidance is clear: shades require no intervention beyond prayer for the departed. They are not suffering. They are not present. They are, as best I can determine, the spiritual equivalent of a scar.

## On Ghosts

This is where my research becomes more difficult to write, and more difficult to read back.

A ghost is not an echo. It is aware. Witnesses consistently describe a sense of being seen, of the figure turning toward them, reaching, sometimes moving objects or producing sounds. Unlike a shade, a ghost responds to the presence of the living.

What disturbs me most in the accounts I have reviewed is this: no ghost has ever communicated clearly. They reach, they knock, they disturb - but nothing coherent passes between them and the living. Aldric suggested, when I raised this with him, that perhaps they are trying. That the inability to communicate is not indifference but limitation.

I have been sitting with that thought for several days now.

The Temple's position is that ghosts are souls unable to complete their passage - held here by attachment, by violence, by something left unresolved. Our role is to pray for their release, to perform the rites of passage that were perhaps denied them, and to trust the gods to do the rest. Whether the gods always answer is not a question I am prepared to examine in writing.

## On the Vampir

I include this entry with significant reservation, as I have found nothing credible to confirm it exists at all. Even among the remote villages they disagree on what to call it. Some refer to it as *strigoi,* others as *upyr,* and even within the Temple's documents there are various spellings of the term.

The vampir appears in accounts from the eastern and northern mountain settlements - always secondhand, always someone's cousin or a merchant who passed through. The description is consistent enough to be either true or a very persistent story: a dead thing that moves, that feeds on the living in some fashion, that is difficult to kill by conventional means. Some in the remote regions are said to make offerings to the creature as a form of worship.

I have raised this with Aldric. He told me to write it down and stop asking him about it.

I have written it down.

## On the Corpus

I am even more skeptical here than I was with the strigoi, and I was quite skeptical there.

The accounts describe animated dead - skeletons walking, the newly buried rising. They come exclusively from places no one goes anymore: collapsed mining settlements, abandoned frontier outposts, the edges of the Frozen Wastes. In every case the account is old, unverified, and passed through enough hands to be unrecognizable from whatever truth it originated from.

My considered opinion, having reviewed what I could find, is that the majority of these accounts describe something far more mundane and far more terrible: starvation. Communities cut off from supply, reduced to doing what people do when they have nothing left. The dead do not walk. People do. And people, when desperate enough, do things that the survivors cannot bring themselves to describe plainly.

I note this not to be unkind to the accounts, but because I believe the Temple serves no one by chasing shadows when the real horror is entirely human.

## On the Subject of Callers

I almost did not include this section. I am including it because Aldric specifically asked me to, and because I think my reluctance is itself informative.

A Caller is not like the others. A shade is a remnant. A ghost is a soul. A Caller, if the accounts are to be believed, is neither - or rather, it is many, compressed into something that believes itself to be one.

It originates, inconsistently, in places of mass death. Battlefields. Fallen settlements. Sites of plague. The accounts suggest that when enough souls fail to complete their passage in the same place at the same time, something forms from the aggregate - a presence that is not any single person but carries the weight of all of them.

What it does with that weight is where the accounts become difficult to read.

It intrudes. Witnesses describe thoughts that are not their own - a pull, a sense of being called toward somewhere specific. Those who follow do not return. Those who resist describe the experience as though something was dying inside their head and pulling at them as it went.

I believe the Caller is suffering. I believe it knows it is diminishing and does not want to. I do not believe it understands what it is doing to the people it reaches for.

## Physical Description

The stone drake is a heavy-bodied quadruped, roughly twice the mass of large bear species. Its most distinctive feature is a set of short wings that fold so flush against the body — covered in the same dense, grey-brown stone-textured scaling as the rest of the hide — that a motionless drake on a rocky slope reads as geology rather than animal. The wings are not built for sustained flight; they generate enough lift for explosive short-range launches from height or from a crouch. A broad dorsal ridge of calcified bone plates runs from the neck to the tail, terminating in outward-angled spurs. The eyes are amber-gold, wide-set, with a vertical slit pupil and a patience in the gaze that observers consistently describe before they describe anything else.

## Wild Behavior

Stone drakes are ambush predators that do not pursue prey at sustained speed. They locate a position above a game trail, river crossing, or open approach, press flat, and wait. The attack is a drop — several hundred pounds of stone-plated animal from elevation, wings deploying on impact to pin the target. They are solitary, territorial, and concentrated in difficult terrain where bare rock provides ideal cover. They will predate on most creatures in their habitat, and have been known to raid unprotected human settlements on occasion.

## The Temple

We are the blessed.  
We are not raised to serve a single god, but to bear witness to the multitude.  
No house shall claim the sky alone. No altar closes its doors against a face it does not know.  
We are the table at which every god can sup. We are the shelter under which every god can rest.  
We do not apologize for our purpose. We gather what would otherwise scatter, and keep what might be forgotten. We stand between the people and the worship of false idols – the nameless things that shall not find respite under our watch.  
O’ brothers and sisters, friend and foe, remember that our generosity is wide, but do not mistake our kindness.  
We pursue our enemies until we overtake them. We do not stop until they are destroyed.  
Gods be praised!  

## The Order  

O’ faithful servants.  
Clerics of the Order.  
We must always show ourselves faithful to the faithful.  
We must always show ourselves pure to the pure.  
We must always show ourselves humble to the humble.  
But to the blasphemer, to the corrupt, to the wicked, we show ourselves to be just. For we carry the strength of the gods where our feet fall, and where mercy is called for, we give it. Where vengeance is called for, we give it.  
Go in faith brothers and sisters, and let no enemy find peace under the eyes of the gods.  
Gods be praised!

## Decrees  

O’ brothers, we serve the many gods!  
The gods of the Temple are the true gods!
We must be careful to avoid offense!  
We must not worship gods that do not find rest in the Temple!
We must not murder unjustly, for to take away their children is an affront to the gods.  
We must not violate the sanctity of another’s body, for the body is an extension of the Temple and therefore sacred.  
A man may not take another man as property, for we belong to the gods and no one can take what belongs to the heavens.  
A marriage is sacred when blessed by the gods, another man may not lay between man and wife or with the wife alone.  
Husbands should respect their wives and hold them sacred, for women are the gateway through which souls enter the world.  
Wives should respect their husbands and hold them sacred, for husbands are the hand of the gods who keep evil at bay.  
Always protect the soul, for though it inhabits the body, it is borne of the gods and therefore does not die with it.  
Respect the fallen dead, lest they return to extract a vengeance denied in life.  
O’ brothers and sisters, hold your oaths sacred and do not let your tongue fail.  
O’ brothers and sisters, humble yourselves before the gods.  
Trouble yourselves not with the world and material things, for those who suffer best are favored by the gods.  
Gods be praised!  

## Condemnation of the Old Gods

We repent! O’ gods!  
We renounce the worship of the old ways.  
Of the gods who shared our flaws.  
Gods who lacked purity and morality.  
Gods consumed by greed and lust.  
O’ brothers and sisters, no more!  
Seek first the Temple and learn what is true.  
To continue to walk a wrong path is to demand judgement, and the gods will not find mercy on those who stray.  
Gods be praised!

## Condemnation of Nature Worship

We have brought order to chaos.  
We have brought justice to the unjust world.  
Yet there are those who still deny what they can plainly see.  
Those who worship the sky, or the trees, or the beasts that crawl on the land.  
They pray to a mountain or the sea.  
O’ they are blind!  
Do they not hear the gods speak with the wind?  
Do they not see the love of the gods in the eyes of the dog?  
No!  
They seek to become one with the beasts!  
They would deny their place as the favored.  
They reject the gods and worship the wild.  
O’ they shall not find mercy among us, and be hunted like the beasts they are.  
Gods be praised!

## Condemnation for the Occult

Unclean souls!  
We have driven the fires from the near hills, yet the worship persists! 
O’ brothers and sisters, there are those among us who set tables in low places.  
What gods do you think partake at these tables?  
False gods!  
Spirits who inhabit temples languishing in darkness.  
Blasphemers who feed the dead and call it tribute.  
O’ how they know not what they do.  
How they bring curses upon the living.  
We say the dead are dead.  
We deny them the blood they seek.  
O’ how the fires shall cleanse their wayward souls.  
Gods be praised!
